sections.overview: The common cuttlefish is a cephalopod mollusc of the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. It lives close to the seabed, hunts by ambush and can change its skin colour and texture within seconds. It breeds once and then dies, usually at about two years of age.
sections.identification: The mantle usually measures 30–49 cm depending on the region, with a record of 60 cm, and the body weighs 2–4 kg. An oblong internal shell, the cuttlebone, lies in the mantle. Pigment cells (chromatophores) and light-reflecting cells (leucophores and iridophores) let the skin change; the usual colour is mottled black or brown.
sections.habitat: It lives in the eastern North Atlantic, the English Channel and the Mediterranean, with populations along West Africa as far south as South Africa. It occupies sandy or muddy bottoms from shallow water to 200 m deep, staying inshore in spring and summer and moving to 100–200 m in autumn and winter.
sections.diet: Crustaceans and fish form the bulk of the diet, with some gastropods, nemertean worms, polychaetes and other cuttlefish. It is an ambush predator that either shoots out its two long tentacles or pounces on prey.
sections.behavior: Mostly nocturnal, it spends most of its time on the seafloor and buries itself in sand by day. It changes skin pattern within seconds to blend in, flees by jet propulsion through its siphon and releases ink when threatened. It is solitary except when mating.
sections.reproduction: Spawning takes place in shallow, warmer water in spring and summer; courting males display coloured bands. A female carries from 150 to 4,000 eggs, each 6–9 mm, laid in clusters on seaweed, shells and other supports. Eggs hatch in 30–90 days depending on temperature. In the English Channel the life cycle lasts two years, though a small share of males mature at one year; both sexes die after breeding.
sections.ecology: The common cuttlefish is an active consumer with a broad, flexible niche. It is preyed on by large fish, sharks, dolphins, toothed whales and seals, and defends itself by camouflage, ink and rapid jet escapes.
sections.conservation: The species is believed to be abundant and not threatened with extinction, but fishing is near the maximum sustainable yield. In the English Channel the stock is considered fully exploited, and in 2010–2011 animals matured at a smaller size than in the 1990s, possibly linked to fishing effort and warming seas.
